title: An Improved Global EDF Schedulability Test for Uniform Multiprocessors

extraction.paper_name: An improved global EDF schedulability test for uniform multiprocessors
extraction.paper_description: This paper presents a new sufficient schedulability test for global EDF scheduling of constrained-deadline sporadic task systems on uniform multiprocessor platforms. It quantitatively evaluates the test using processor speedup factors, defining two different metrics for uniform multiprocessors.

formal_description.statement: A sporadic task tau_i is characterized by (C_i, D_i, T_i). It generates an infinite sequence of jobs. Successive jobs arrive at least T_i time units apart. Each job has an execution requirement at most C_i and a deadline D_i time units after its arrival.

variables.C_i: Worst-case execution requirement of task tau_i
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival separation (period) of task tau_i

assumptions: Fully preemptive execution model
Jobs may be interrupted and resumed without cost
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the parameters and behavior of a sporadic task.

informal_sketch.intuition: A sporadic task is a recurring piece of work with a maximum execution time, a deadline relative to its arrival, and a minimum time between consecutive arrivals.
steps: A task `tau_i` is defined by its execution time `C_i`, deadline `D_i`, and period `T_i`.
It can release jobs at any time, but at least `T_i` apart.
Each job needs `C_i` execution and must finish within `D_i` of its arrival.
key_insights: Models recurring, non-periodic real-time workloads.
Parameters define worst-case behavior for analysis.

formal_description.statement: A sporadic task system tau = {tau_1, ..., tau_n} is a constrained sporadic task system if D_i <= T_i for all tau_i in tau.

variables.tau: A sporadic task system (collection of sporadic tasks)

assumptions: Each task tau_i follows the Sporadic Task Model
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific type of sporadic task system where deadlines are no later than periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: In a constrained-deadline system, a task's deadline always falls within its current period, simplifying some analysis compared to arbitrary deadlines.
steps: For every task `tau_i` in the system `tau`:
Check if `tau_i.D` is less than or equal to `tau_i.T`.
If this holds for all tasks, the system is constrained-deadline.
key_insights: Simplifies analysis by ensuring a job's deadline is before the next job of the same task arrives.

formal_description.statement: A uniform multiprocessor platform pi is comprised of m_pi > 1 processors. The i'th-fastest processor has a speed or computing capacity of rho_i_pi. A job executing on the i'th-fastest processor for t time units completes t * rho_i_pi units of execution.

variables.m_pi: Number of processors in platform pi
variables.rho_i_pi: Speed/capacity of the i'th-fastest processor in pi

assumptions: Processors differ only in speed
Global inter-processor migration is allowed
Each job executes on at most one processor at each instant
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a multiprocessor platform where processors can have different speeds.

informal_sketch.intuition: A uniform multiprocessor is a set of CPUs, each potentially running at a different speed. Work done is proportional to the processor's speed.
steps: The platform `pi` has `m_pi` processors.
Each processor `i` has a speed `rho_i_pi`.
If a job runs on processor `i` for `t` time, it completes `t * rho_i_pi` units of work.
key_insights: Generalizes identical multiprocessors by allowing varying processor speeds.
Work completion is directly scaled by processor speed.

formal_description.statement: An identical multiprocessor is a special case of a uniform multiprocessor, in which all the processors have the same speed; without loss of generality, this speed is typically assumed to be equal to one.

variables.rho_i_pi: Speed/capacity of the i'th-fastest processor in pi

assumptions: All processors have the same speed (e.g., rho_i_pi = 1 for all i)
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a multiprocessor platform where all processors are identical.

informal_sketch.intuition: All CPUs are the same speed, usually normalized to 1 unit of work per unit of time.
steps: A platform is identical if all its `rho_i_pi` values are equal.
Often, this common speed is set to 1 for simplicity.
key_insights: A simpler model than uniform multiprocessors, often used as a baseline.

formal_description.statement: R_pi = sum(rho_j_pi for j from 1 to m_pi)

variables.R_pi: Total computing capacity of platform pi
variables.rho_j_pi: Speed/capacity of the j'th-fastest processor in pi
variables.m_pi: Number of processors in platform pi

assumptions: pi is a Uniform Multiprocessor Platform
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the sum of speeds of all processors in a uniform multiprocessor platform.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the total 'horsepower' of the entire multiprocessor platform, summing up the speeds of all its individual processors.
steps: Initialize `total_capacity = 0`.
For each processor `j` from `1` to `m_pi`:
Add `rho_j_pi` to `total_capacity`.
The result is `R_pi`.
key_insights: Represents the maximum amount of work that can be completed per unit of time by the entire platform.

formal_description.statement: lambda_pi = max(sum(rho_j_pi for j from i+1 to m_pi) / rho_i_pi for i from 1 to m_pi)

variables.rho_j_pi: Speed/capacity of the j'th-fastest processor in pi
variables.rho_i_pi: Speed/capacity of the i'th-fastest processor in pi
variables.m_pi: Number of processors in platform pi

assumptions: pi is a Uniform Multiprocessor Platform
Processors are ordered by speed: rho_1_pi >= rho_2_pi >= ... >= rho_m_pi_pi
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a parameter characterizing the 'skewness' or 'non-uniformity' of processor speeds, useful for worst-case analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: The lambda parameter quantifies how much 'idle capacity' can be generated on slower processors while a job is still running on a faster one. It's the maximum ratio of the sum of speeds of all processors slower than `i` to the speed of processor `i` itself, across all processors `i`.
steps: Initialize `max_lambda = 0`.
For each processor `i` from `1` to `m_pi` (assuming `rho_i_pi` is the speed of the `i`-th processor, 1-indexed):
Calculate `sum_slower_speeds = sum(rho_j_pi for j from i+1 to m_pi)`.
If `rho_i_pi` is not zero, calculate `current_lambda = sum_slower_speeds / rho_i_pi`.
Update `max_lambda = max(max_lambda, current_lambda)`.
The result is `lambda_pi`.
key_insights: Captures the worst-case efficiency loss due to processor idling when fewer jobs than processors are active, especially when faster processors are busy and slower ones are idle.
A higher `lambda_pi` indicates greater non-uniformity and potential for idling.

formal_description.statement: With respect to a given platform, a given sporadic task system is said to be feasible if there exists a schedule meeting all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines when a task system can theoretically meet all its deadlines on a given platform.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task system is feasible if it's possible to schedule all its jobs to meet their deadlines, regardless of how they arrive (as long as they follow the sporadic model). This is the 'ideal' schedulability.
steps: Consider all possible job arrival sequences allowed by the sporadic task model.
For each sequence, determine if *any* scheduling algorithm (even an optimal, clairvoyant one) can ensure all jobs complete by their deadlines.
If such an algorithm exists for all sequences, the system is feasible.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_feasible(task_system, platform):
    # This is a theoretical concept, not directly computable for arbitrary systems.
    # It implies the existence of an optimal scheduler.
    # For analysis, we often use necessary conditions for feasibility.
    pass
key_insights: Feasibility is the ultimate goal; schedulability tests are approximations of feasibility.
An optimal scheduler is assumed to achieve feasibility.

formal_description.statement: A given sporadic task system is said to be (global) EDF schedulable if EDF meets all deadlines for every collection of jobs that may be generated by the task system.
assumptions: EDF scheduling algorithm is used
Global inter-processor migration is allowed
formal_description.conclusion: Defines when a task system can meet all its deadlines specifically under global EDF scheduling.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task system is EDF schedulable if the Earliest Deadline First algorithm can successfully schedule all its jobs to meet their deadlines.
steps: Apply the EDF scheduling algorithm to the given `task_system` on the `platform`.
Simulate or analyze all possible job arrival sequences.
If EDF ensures all jobs complete by their deadlines for all sequences, the system is EDF schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_edf_schedulable(task_system, platform):
    # This is what schedulability tests aim to determine.
    # It's a property of the (task_system, platform, EDF_algorithm) triplet.
    pass
key_insights: EDF schedulability is a practical goal, as EDF is a widely used and often near-optimal algorithm.
Schedulability tests provide sufficient (and sometimes necessary) conditions for EDF schedulability.

results.identifier: FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma - Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function (single task)

formal_description.statement:
q_i = floor(t / T_i)
r_i = t - q_i * T_i
FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma = q_i * C_i + (C_i if r_i >= D_i else (C_i - (D_i - r_i) * sigma if D_i > r_i >= D_i - C_i * sigma else 0))

variables.sigma: A processor speed parameter (positive real number, C_i/D_i <= sigma <= 1)
variables.C_i: Worst-case execution requirement of task tau_i
variables.q_i: Number of full periods of tau_i within t
variables.r_i: Remaining time in t after q_i full periods

assumptions: tau_i is a Sporadic Task
C_i / D_i <= sigma <= 1
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum execution demand of a single task tau_i over an interval of length t, considering execution outside the interval on a speed-sigma processor.

informal_sketch.intuition: This function calculates the maximum amount of work a single task `tau_i` can demand within a time interval `t`, assuming any 'carry-in' or 'carry-out' work (jobs partially executing outside `t`) is done on a processor of speed `sigma`. It accounts for full jobs within `t` and a partial job straddling the interval boundary.
steps: Calculate `q_i`, the number of full `T_i` periods that fit into `t`.
Calculate `r_i`, the remainder of `t` after `q_i` periods.
The base demand is `q_i * C_i` (for `q_i` full jobs).
Consider an additional job that might straddle the interval boundary:
If `r_i >= D_i`, this job's deadline is within `t`, so it demands `C_i`.

If `D_i > r_i >= D_i - C_i * sigma`, this job's deadline is outside `t`, but it needs `C_i` execution. It can complete `(D_i - r_i) * sigma` units outside `t` on a speed-`sigma` processor. So, its demand within `t` is `C_i - (D_i - r_i) * sigma`.
Otherwise (if `r_i < D_i - C_i * sigma`), the job can complete entirely outside `t` or its demand within `t` is 0.
Sum the base demand and the additional job's demand.
key_insights: Models demand for a task when its execution might span across the interval boundary, with a 'forced-forward' assumption about execution outside the interval.
The `sigma` parameter allows modeling different scenarios for how 'carry-in' or 'carry-out' jobs are handled.

results.identifier: delta_max_tau - Maximum Density of a Task System

formal_description.statement: delta_max_tau = max(C_i / D_i for tau_i in tau)

variables.delta_max_tau: Maximum density of task system tau
variables.C_i: Worst-case execution requirement of task tau_i

assumptions: tau is a Sporadic Task System
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum individual task density within a task system.

informal_sketch.intuition: The density `C_i / D_i` represents the minimum processor speed required for a single task `tau_i` to meet its deadline if it runs continuously. `delta_max_tau` is the highest such requirement among all tasks in the system.
steps: Initialize `max_density = 0`.
For each task `tau_i` in `tau`:
Calculate `current_density = tau_i.C / tau_i.D`.
Update `max_density = max(max_density, current_density)`.
The result is `delta_max_tau`.
key_insights: A necessary condition for schedulability: the fastest processor must be able to handle the task with the highest density.
Often used as a lower bound for processor speed in analysis.

results.identifier: FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma - Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function (task system)

formal_description.statement: FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma = sum(FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma for tau_i in tau)

variables.FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma: Total forced-forward demand of task system tau
variables.FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma: Forced-forward demand of single task tau_i

assumptions: tau is a Sporadic Task System
FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma is defined for each task
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total maximum execution demand of all tasks in a system over an interval of length t, under the forced-forward assumption.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the sum of the individual `FF_DBF` values for all tasks in the system. It represents the total work demanded by the entire task system within an interval `t`, considering the `sigma` speed for carry-in/out jobs.
steps: Initialize `total_demand = 0`.
For each task `tau_i` in `tau`:
Calculate `task_demand = compute_ff_dbf_single_task(tau_i, t, sigma)`.
Add `task_demand` to `total_demand`.
The result is `FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma`.
key_insights: Aggregates the demand of individual tasks to get the system-wide demand.
Crucial for multiprocessor schedulability analysis, as it represents the total work that needs to be completed.

dependencies: FF_DBF_tau_i_t_sigma - Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function (single task)

formal_description.statement: FF_LOAD_tau_sigma = max(FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma / t for t > 0)

variables.FF_LOAD_tau_sigma: Forced-forward load of task system tau
variables.FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma: Total forced-forward demand of task system tau

assumptions: tau is a Sporadic Task System
FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma is defined
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum average demand rate (load) of a task system over any interval, considering the forced-forward assumption.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the maximum 'utilization' or 'load' that the task system can impose on the processors, considering all possible interval lengths `t` and the `sigma` speed for carry-in/out jobs. It's the peak demand-to-time ratio.
steps: Iterate over all possible positive interval lengths `t` (in practice, a finite set of critical points).
For each `t`, calculate `current_load = compute_ff_dbf_system(tau, t, sigma) / t`.
Find the maximum `current_load` over all `t`.
The result is `FF_LOAD_tau_sigma`.
key_insights: Represents the worst-case instantaneous load that the system can generate.
A critical metric for schedulability tests, as it must be bounded by the platform's capacity.

dependencies: FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma - Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function (task system)

formal_description.statement: FF_DBF_tau_L_s >= sum(W_i for i from 1 to k)

variables.FF_DBF_tau_L_s: Forced-forward demand of task system tau over interval L with speed s
variables.W_i: Total amount of execution occurring over the interval [t_i, t_i-1)
variables.k: Index of the first job in the critical sequence

assumptions: tau is a Constrained-Deadline Sporadic Task System
L = t_o - t_k
W_i is the total execution in [t_i, t_i-1)
All jobs contributing to sum(W_i) have deadlines within [t_k, t_o)
formal_description.conclusion: The total forced-forward demand of the task system over the critical interval [t_k, t_o) is an upper bound on the actual work done by jobs that contribute to the deadline miss.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a deadline is missed, we can identify a critical interval `[t_k, t_o)` where a lot of work was demanded. This lemma states that the total demand calculated by `FF_DBF` for the entire task system over this interval is at least as much as the actual work done by the jobs that were active and contributed to the deadline miss within sub-intervals `[t_i, t_i-1)`.
steps: Identify a critical interval `L = t_o - t_k` where a deadline miss occurs.
Define `W_i` as the work done in sub-intervals `[t_i, t_i-1)` within `L`.
The `FF_DBF` function is designed to capture the maximum possible demand from tasks.
Since all jobs contributing to `sum(W_i)` have deadlines within `L`, their total demand is bounded by `FF_DBF_tau_L_s`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_lemma_1_1(task_system, L, s, actual_work_segments):
    # This lemma is part of a proof by contradiction.
    # It establishes a relationship between theoretical demand and actual work.
    theoretical_demand = compute_ff_dbf_system(task_system, L, s)
    actual_total_work = sum(actual_work_segments)
    return theoretical_demand >= actual_total_work
key_insights: Connects the theoretical demand bound function to the actual execution observed in a failing schedule.
Forms a crucial part of the proof for the schedulability test by bounding the total work.

dependencies: FF_DBF_tau_t_sigma - Forced-Forward Demand Bound Function (task system)

formal_description.statement: W_i > (t_i_minus_1 - t_i) * (R_pi - s * lambda_pi)

variables.W_i: Total amount of execution occurring over the interval [t_i, t_i-1)
variables.R_pi: Total computing capacity of platform pi

assumptions: pi is a Uniform Multiprocessor Platform
A job j_i does not complete execution by t_i_minus_1
EDF scheduling rules for uniform multiprocessors are followed (faster processors used first)
The amount of execution job j_i receives over [t_i, t_i-1) is less than (t_i_minus_1 - t_i) * s
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a lower bound on the actual work done in a sub-interval [t_i, t_i-1) during a deadline miss scenario.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma quantifies the minimum amount of work that *must* have been done by the processors in a sub-interval `[t_i, t_i-1)` if a job `j_i` is still active but hasn't completed. It accounts for the total processor capacity `R_pi` and subtracts the maximum possible 'wasted' capacity due to idling, which is related to `s * lambda_pi`.
steps: In a deadline miss scenario, a job `j_i` is active but not completed.
Due to EDF rules on uniform multiprocessors, faster processors are always used if jobs are available.
The total work done in `[t_i, t_i-1)` is `(t_i_minus_1 - t_i) * R_pi` minus any idled capacity.
The maximum idled capacity is bounded by `(t_i_minus_1 - t_i) * s * lambda_pi` (this is the key insight from the lambda parameter's definition in the appendix).
Subtracting this maximum idled capacity gives a lower bound on `W_i`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_min_work_in_interval(interval_length, platform_R, s_param, platform_lambda):
    # This is a theoretical lower bound derived from the properties of EDF on uniform multiprocessors.
    min_work = interval_length * (platform_R - s_param * platform_lambda)
    return min_work
key_insights: Leverages the `lambda_pi` parameter to bound the maximum amount of processor capacity that can be idled while a job is still active.
Crucial for establishing a lower bound on the actual work performed in a critical interval, which is then compared against the demand.

formal_description.statement: Suppose that constrained_deadline_sporadic_task_system_tau is NOT EDF_schedulable upon uniform_multiprocessor_platform_pi. Then for each sigma, sigma >= delta_max_tau, FF_LOAD_tau_sigma > R_pi - sigma * lambda_pi.

variables.delta_max_tau: Maximum density of task system tau
variables.FF_LOAD_tau_sigma: Forced-forward load of task system tau
variables.R_pi: Total computing capacity of platform pi

assumptions: tau is a Constrained-Deadline Sporadic Task System
tau is NOT EDF_schedulable on pi
sigma >= delta_max_tau
formal_description.conclusion: If a task system is not EDF-schedulable, then its forced-forward load must exceed a specific platform capacity metric for any valid sigma.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem provides a necessary condition for a deadline miss under global EDF on uniform multiprocessors. If a system fails to be schedulable, it implies that at some point, the demand (FF-LOAD) must have exceeded the effective capacity of the platform (R_pi - sigma * lambda_pi), considering the potential for idling.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that `tau` is not EDF-schedulable.
Identify a minimal sequence of jobs leading to a deadline miss at `t_o` for job `j_1`.
Construct a critical interval `[t_k, t_o)` and a sequence of jobs `j_i` and arrival times `t_i` (as described in the paper's proof).
Apply Lemma 1.1: `FF_DBF_tau_L_s >= sum(W_i)`.
Apply Lemma 1.2: `sum(W_i) > sum((t_i_minus_1 - t_i) * (R_pi - s * lambda_pi))`.
Combine these to show `FF_DBF_tau_L_s > (R_pi - s * lambda_pi) * L`.
Since `FF_LOAD_tau_s` is defined as `max(FF_DBF_tau_t_s / t)`, it must be that `FF_LOAD_tau_s >= FF_DBF_tau_L_s / L`.
Therefore, `FF_LOAD_tau_s > R_pi - s * lambda_pi`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def prove_theorem_1_by_contradiction(task_system, platform, sigma_param):
    # This is a proof, not an algorithm to run.
    # It shows that if EDF fails, then a specific load condition must be true.
    # The proof involves constructing a 'failing' schedule and analyzing work done.
    # Key steps involve applying Lemma 1.1 and Lemma 1.2 to bound demand and work.
    pass
key_insights: Establishes a fundamental relationship between task system demand, platform capacity, and schedulability failure.
The term `R_pi - sigma * lambda_pi` represents the 'effective' capacity of the uniform multiprocessor under EDF, accounting for potential idling due to non-uniform speeds.
Forms the basis for the sufficient schedulability test (Theorem 2).

dependencies: delta_max_tau - Maximum Density of a Task System

formal_description.statement: Constrained_deadline_sporadic_task_system_tau is EDF_schedulable upon uniform_multiprocessor_platform_pi IF there exists a sigma >= delta_max_tau, such that FF_LOAD_tau_sigma <= R_pi - sigma * lambda_pi.

variables.delta_max_tau: Maximum density of task system tau
variables.FF_LOAD_tau_sigma: Forced-forward load of task system tau
variables.R_pi: Total computing capacity of platform pi

assumptions: tau is a Constrained-Deadline Sporadic Task System
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a sufficient condition for EDF schedulability on uniform multiprocessors.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the main schedulability test. If we can find *any* `sigma` (a hypothetical processor speed for carry-in/out jobs) such that the system's maximum demand rate (`FF_LOAD`) is less than or equal to the platform's effective capacity (`R_pi - sigma * lambda_pi`), then the system is guaranteed to be EDF-schedulable.
steps: Iterate through a range of possible `sigma` values, starting from `delta_max_tau`.
For each `sigma`:
Calculate `FF_LOAD_tau_sigma` using the definitions.
Calculate the platform's effective capacity: `effective_capacity = R_pi - sigma * lambda_pi`.
If `FF_LOAD_tau_sigma <= effective_capacity`, then the system is schedulable.
If no such `sigma` is found after checking all relevant values, the test is inconclusive (it's a sufficient test, not exact).
key_insights: Directly derived from the negation of Theorem 1.
Provides a practical way to check schedulability by comparing demand (FF-LOAD) against a capacity metric that accounts for processor non-uniformity.
The choice of `sigma` is crucial; finding an optimal `sigma` might involve numerical search or specific analytical solutions.

dependencies: delta_max_tau - Maximum Density of a Task System

formal_description.statement: If FF_LOAD_tau_sigma > m_sigma then tau is NOT feasible on m speed_sigma processors.

variables.FF_LOAD_tau_sigma: Forced-forward load of task system tau
variables.m_sigma: Total capacity of m processors each of speed sigma (i.e., m * sigma)

assumptions: tau is a Sporadic Task System
formal_description.conclusion: If the forced-forward load exceeds the total capacity of an identical multiprocessor platform (m processors of speed sigma), then the task system is not feasible on that platform.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a basic necessary condition for feasibility. If the maximum demand rate (`FF_LOAD`) of a task system is greater than the total processing capacity (`m * sigma`) of an identical multiprocessor platform, then it's impossible to meet all deadlines, even with an optimal scheduler.
steps: Assume `FF_LOAD_tau_sigma > m * sigma`.
By definition of `FF_LOAD`, there exists an interval `t_o` such that `FF_DBF_tau_t_o_sigma / t_o = FF_LOAD_tau_sigma`.
This implies `FF_DBF_tau_t_o_sigma > m * sigma * t_o`.
The term `m * sigma * t_o` represents the total work that `m` speed-`sigma` processors can do in `t_o` time.
Since the total demand `FF_DBF_tau_t_o_sigma` exceeds the total available work, a deadline must be missed, meaning the system is not feasible.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_infeasibility_identical_mp(task_system, m_processors, sigma_speed):
    critical_t_values = get_critical_t_values(task_system) # Or a sufficiently large set
    ff_load = compute_ff_load(task_system, sigma_speed, critical_t_values)
    platform_capacity = m_processors * sigma_speed
    if ff_load > platform_capacity:
        return True # Infeasible
    return False # May be feasible
key_insights: A fundamental lower bound on the required processor capacity for feasibility.
Highlights that `FF_LOAD` can be used as a measure of system demand against platform capacity.

formal_description.statement: If task_system_tau fails to satisfy Condition 4 of Theorem 2, then it is infeasible upon a platform comprised of m_pi processors each of speed R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi).

variables.m_pi: Number of processors in platform pi
variables.R_pi: Total computing capacity of platform pi

assumptions: tau is a Constrained-Deadline Sporadic Task System
tau fails Condition 4 of Theorem 2 (i.e., for each s >= delta_max_tau, FF_LOAD_tau_s > R_pi - s * lambda_pi)
formal_description.conclusion: If the schedulability test of Theorem 2 fails for a task system, then that task system is infeasible on a specific slower identical multiprocessor platform.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma connects the failure of our EDF schedulability test (Theorem 2) to the infeasibility on a *hypothetically slower* identical multiprocessor platform. It's a step towards quantifying the test's pessimism using speedup factors.
steps: Assume `tau` fails Theorem 2's condition: `FF_LOAD_tau_s > R_pi - s * lambda_pi` for all relevant `s`.
Choose a specific `s = R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)`.
Substitute this `s` into the inequality: `FF_LOAD_tau_s > R_pi - (R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)) * lambda_pi`.
Simplify the right-hand side: `R_pi * (1 - lambda_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)) = R_pi * (m_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)) = m_pi * (R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi))`.
So, `FF_LOAD_tau_s > m_pi * s` (where `s` is the chosen speed).
By Lemma 1 (Section 4.1), if `FF_LOAD_tau_s > m_pi * s`, then `tau` is infeasible on `m_pi` processors each of speed `s`.
Thus, `tau` is infeasible on `m_pi` processors each of speed `R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_lemma_2_infeasibility(task_system, platform):
    # This is a theoretical derivation for the speedup factor proof.
    # It shows that if our test fails, the system is 'really' infeasible on a slower platform.
    # The speed of the slower identical processors is calculated as:
    s_prime = platform.R / (platform.m + platform.lambda_param)
    # The lemma states that if the test fails, then FF_LOAD(tau, s_prime) > platform.m * s_prime

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem states that if our EDF schedulability test (Theorem 2) says a task system is NOT schedulable on a uniform multiprocessor `pi`, then even an optimal scheduler couldn't schedule it on an identical multiprocessor platform that is `1 / (1 + lambda_pi / m_pi)` times slower. This factor `1 + lambda_pi / m_pi` is the speedup factor.
steps: From Lemma 2 (Section 4.1), if `tau` fails Theorem 2, it is infeasible on `m_pi` processors each of speed `R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)`.
The total capacity of this slower identical platform is `m_pi * (R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi))`.
The total capacity of the original uniform platform `pi` is `R_pi`.
The ratio of the original platform's capacity to the slower platform's capacity is the speedup factor:
`R_pi / (m_pi * (R_pi / (m_pi + lambda_pi)))`
`= R_pi * (m_pi + lambda_pi) / (m_pi * R_pi)`
`= (m_pi + lambda_pi) / m_pi`
`= 1 + lambda_pi / m_pi`.

    return 1 + platform.lambda_param / platform.m

If a system is feasible, the task with the highest density (`delta_max_tau`) must be able to run on the fastest processor (`rho_1_pi_o`). From the definition of `lambda_pi_o`, it can be shown that `rho_1_pi_o <= R_pi_o / (1 + lambda_pi_o)`.
Combining these two inequalities yields `delta_max_tau <= R_pi_o / (1 + lambda_pi_o)`.

From Lemma 4, since `tau` is feasible on `pi_o`, `FF_LOAD_tau_s_prime <= R_pi_o`.
Combine these: `R_pi_o > R_pi - s_prime * lambda_pi`.
Substitute `R_pi = C * R_pi_o` and `s_prime = R_pi_o / (1 + lambda_pi_o)` and `lambda_pi = lambda_pi_o` (from problem setup):
`R_pi_o > C * R_pi_o - (R_pi_o / (1 + lambda_pi_o)) * lambda_pi_o`.
Divide by `R_pi_o`: `1 > C - lambda_pi_o / (1 + lambda_pi_o)`.
Rearrange: `C < 1 + lambda_pi_o / (1 + lambda_pi_o) = (1 + 2 * lambda_pi_o) / (1 + lambda_pi_o)`.
